item.title: Bishopsgate Institute keeps it kinky!
item.description:
Example of physique photography in the Bishopsgate Institute archive

Photography historian Annebella Pollen consults Stefan Dickers and the queer collections of Bishopsgate Institute, an archive in which all predilections are welcome

“Watch out,” archivist Stefan Dickers remarks, as we manoeuvre our way around a Victorian library, past piles of papers awaiting processing. “There are willies on the table.”

The body parts in question are among a sprawling new deposit of materials relating to Operation Spanner, the 1987–1990 police investigation into same-sex male sadomasochism which tested the legal limits of sexual consent. Specifically, amid this abundant paperwork, the willies are on show in a pile of gay porn magazines from the 1980s. We leaf through lavishly illustrated copies of Him, each issue bursting with colour photographs of smooth and muscular naked men, posing in an imaginative variety of sexual positions. Incongruously, they all have flaccid penises. The magazines had to toe the line on obscenity law to stay in business.

Much of the material Dickers rates shows rather less restraint. A self-confessed pervert as well as an experienced archivist, Dickers has spent 20 years at Bishopsgate Institute, near Liverpool Street station in London, transforming it from a long-standing repository, mostly known only to historians interested in London life, to what it is today – an international magnet for the collection and preservation of records of queer sexual pleasures and related LGBTQIA+ community engagement.

Especially since 2016, when Dickers launched the kink collections, the institute’s archive has shifted radically. In reflection of its holdings, the reading room is now festooned with multicoloured Pride flags and mirrored mannequins; researchers consult their files alongside nightclub remnants, including a human-shaped iron gibbet cage from former east London leather bar, The Backstreet.

“I’m not poring over photographs considering their ‘compositional merit’… I’m interested in the social history of the photograph – what tropes it shows, what ideals, what communities and what practices” – Stefan Dickers

The success of his experiment is backed up by numbers, with thousands of visitors flocking to consult the LGBTQIA+ material each year. One in-person event, Kink in the Archives, sold 500 tickets in just two hours. “Every day, people come to browse material who have never previously entered an archive,” says Dickers. “Every day, people bring objects to deposit that otherwise wouldn’t find a willing home.” I see this in action soon after we discuss it. A man in his sixties bends the ear of the staff about his life as he draws ring binders from a plastic bag.

Dickers is dressed all in black. He wears a tweed flat cap and an enduring mischievous twinkle in his eye. This is a man who loves his job and can speak endlessly and passionately about his mission. Quick to laugh, he has an amusing Les Dawson-like habit of dramatically whispering when mentioning “unmentionables”. Unsurprisingly, given the nature of his interests, unmentionables frequently take conversational centre stage.

“Help yourself to any items on the trolley,” he says encouragingly as I eye a stash of 1980s magazines, selected to provide a mixed taster for those unsure where to begin, with 14 storerooms crammed with leather harnesses, latex boots, scholarly tomes, how-to manuals and photographs. I peruse copies of Rubber Lovers: A Profusion of Rubber Delights; Rubber Quarterly (International Edition) and The Best of Rubber Life. These contain, as might be expected, photograph after photograph of young female models wearing skin-tight scanty garments – and, perhaps more surprisingly, portrayals of practical rainwear, perfectly suited to the wet day of my visit.

“Every archive is a reflection of its archivist,” states Dickers, certain that his predilections inform what he collects. But he is also adamant that the Bishopsgate archive is for everyone (as long as they are over 18). The new collections attract new kinds of engagement, even empowerment, and the visual material is an important part of this. “The depiction of sexuality became more visually arresting and spectacular from the 1970s on,” Dickers says, “especially in pornographic magazines.”

Older producers and collectors of print periodicals are passing away or passing them on, and younger generations are intrigued. The illustrated magazine is unfamiliar to those in their twenties, as the contemporary medium for such content is almost solely digital. Like the revival of interest in vinyl records and VHS cassettes among those too young to remember their mundane ubiquity, these visitors are fascinated by the laborious rigmarole required to access the sexual culture of the recent past, its network of cult publications and its clandestine distribution hubs. 

“I’ve been privileged to create an archive from scratch,” Dickers says. Most archivists do not have the resources to do this, but he has both vision and budget. Bishopsgate Institute is relatively well-off, with endowments established by the Christian Church dating back 500 years. Those founding finances now support different kinds of devotion, and visitors come not only to discover the past, but to make new culture with it. “We have young activists coming to create new campaigns inspired by earlier examples. Tattoo artists come to revive historic designs. Young queer people can see that they’ve always been here; there were people like them long before them,” says Dickers.

Photography, to Dickers, is not interesting for aesthetic reasons. “I’m not poring over photographs considering their ‘compositional merit’,” he says, adopting the tones of a patrician art historian. “Neither am I interested in analysing it academically for the semiotics of the image. I’m interested in the social history of the photograph – what tropes it shows, what ideals, what communities and what practices.”

Bishopsgate Institute holds photographic prints as well as magazines, and explicit queer images come to it from all directions. Sometimes the origins are surprising – as in the case of two amateur albums, including the most graphic gay male photographs Dickers had ever seen. The albums had been compiled by the relatives of a donor, and the images were shot in domestic living rooms of the 1940s. “That’s more important to me than photographs by famous people,” Dickers explains, “although we have that too.”

Commercial markets are expanding for famous queer photographers’ work, so Dickers is touched when it is freely donated. The growing attention given to this kind of material – as seen in The Photographers’ Gallery 2023 show A Hard Man is Good to Find!, curated by Alistair O’Neill – has brought major prominence to its leading producers. “There’s now a huge collector market for some of these photographers, such as John S Barrington and Cain of London,” says Dickers. “Physique photography goes for a lot of money now, hundreds of pounds a print.”

Dickers always understood the historic value of photography. Starting his role at Bishopsgate in 2005, he could see the local area evolving fast, as the East End gentrified and new buildings replaced the old. “From about 2006, every six months for about three years, I made the archive assistants take photographs of the surrounding area,” he says. “It was a period of rapid change in London, and we mapped that. That is already a valuable document of transformation.”

These days Dickers dedicates more time to caring for other people’s photographs than creating his own, and he admits that Bishopsgate “has become more of a photography archive than I ever intended”. The institute has developed a reputation for photography, which is partly self-perpetuating. If one photographer places their archive, word quickly spreads to others seeking homes for their work. But also, importantly, the copyright remains with the photographers. “We don’t make any money when the images are used,” says Dickers. 

Not all of the photography archives relate to kink or the LGBTQIA+ community, with Bishopsgate aiming to document both everyday life and those who have campaigned for social, political and cultural change. Format, the radical female photographic agency, which ran from 1983 to 2003, stores its archival prints at Bishopsgate, for example, ensuring the photographs are safe but retaining reproduction fees. Format’s work was recently exhibited at Tate Britain, in the exhibition Women in Revolt: Art and Activism in the UK 1970–1990.

As we roll back the racks of endless publications – Swish for spanking; Forced Womanhood for bondage – my eyes alight on a set of scrapbooks with covers familiar from my childhood. These versions have very different content to my compilations of birthday cards and pictures snipped from comics. They represent the private trove of an elderly former member of the Conservative Party although, in a donation brokered by the rubber fetishists of the Mackintosh Society, the collector’s name was never revealed to Dickers. He was merely dubbed Codename Adam. 

The dozen or so scrapbooks comprehensively document any image of a woman dressed in rubber or plastic from around 1960 to 2000, many of which have come from mainstream sources, such as mail-order clothes catalogues and tabloid newspapers. Some subject matter seems wholly unerotic, such as sou’wester hats and knee-length waterproofs. The scrapbooks’ insistent singularity and meticulousness is impressive; they are simultaneously boring and fascinating.

And therein lies a paradox about material designed for sexual stimulation because, when there are 14 storerooms full of it, excitement can turn to tedium. I view a collection of Mike Arlen photographs of beautiful young men with huge spurting cocks, but they blur into visual noise because of their sheer number. My eyes drift to the patterned carpets and wallpaper of their domestic environments. Historic pornography, I note, frequently features an antiquated television in the background. I marvel at the curiosity of socks and shoes, the only items of clothing left on. Dickers has heard this observation before; it is a professional condition. “Colleagues get anaesthetised to the penis,” he says. 

Dickers cannot be accused of ennui, however. A passionate advocate of archives, he is inspiring a new generation to take up a profession they might not otherwise have known or been enthused by. “When I grew up, I couldn’t see this kind of stuff recorded anywhere,” he tells me. “Consequently, I couldn’t see myself. So I feel I want to pull it together for a new generation.”

Importantly, the archive is not only dedicated to preserving old material: “We also put out calls for contemporary photographers and content creators.” Kinky contemporary performers can deposit their photographs in the archives, and they do so with enthusiasm from all around the world. What are the limits? “Very few,” says Dickers. “We don’t judge aesthetically. We don’t restrict how much photographers can donate. They might select their best five prints, or they might submit 20,000 digital files.”

With permissive attitudes to archival content, Dickers and his team are similarly easy-going about welcoming visitors. No appointment is needed; just wander in. “The archive has been queered, not only in terms of sexuality, but also in terms of form,” says Dickers. “We recently accepted 250,000 bondage photographs generated by the US-based Centurian publishing company, established in 1969. We take vinyl records, we take gas masks, we even take human tissue,” he notes, signalling the remnants of gender-affirming top surgery. 

As I depart, the final shelves are stocked with Boyz magazine, a free London paper packed with pin-up photographs and pick-up ads, typically collected by gay London clubbers at the end of a night out. Published from 1991 to 2024, it is now clothbound into blue library volumes, with gold-tooled titles and dates on the spines. The magazine’s position in the archive formalises the informal. It demonstrates, materially, that the ephemeral visual culture of passing sexual pleasures is as worthy of record as the most traditionally consecrated historical scripts.

The post Peak Design Rethinks the Traditional L-Bracket with New Field Bracket System appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The Kickstarter for Peak Design’s new Field-Bracket is off and running, you can check it out here. Meanwhile, here’s the press release for you to have a gander at;

San Francisco, CA (July 21st, 2026) – Peak Design, Peak Design, a global leader in camera accessories and everyday carry solutions, is proud to announce Field Bracket, a modular L-bracket system that eliminates many of the compromises of traditional L-brackets. While L-brackets have become indispensable for quickly switching between portrait and landscape tripod shooting, they’ve remained largely unchanged, fixed in form, and often at odds with the rest of a photographer’s kit. Peak Design’s Field Bracket rethinks this accessory category with a modular design that adapts as photographers’ needs change.

At the heart of Field Bracket is a camera-specific baseplate precision-machined from recycled aluminum to hug the contours of each supported camera body. Using Peak Design’s custom Field Latch mechanism, photographers can attach or remove Field Bracket’s upright in seconds without tools, transforming the system from a low-profile baseplate into a full L-bracket for portrait tripod shooting. The upright can also be repositioned to provide clearance for tethering and other connected cables, allowing photographers to keep their camera mounted on a tripod without disrupting their workflow.

What currently fits?

Field Bracket serves as the foundation for an expandable system. The optional Beacon Finder Tag is the first tracker specifically designed to fit inside an Arca-compatible camera plate, offering a discreet way to help locate and secure camera gear without the bulk of conventional tracking solutions. For added versatility, photographers can replace Field Bracket’s upright with the optional Cheese Plate, creating a lightweight rig with 1/4″-20, 3/8″-16, and cold shoe mounting points for lights, microphones, monitors, and other accessories. For handheld shooting, users can also add the optional Hand Strap, which integrates directly with Field Bracket to provide greater comfort and security. Across the system, Field Bracket preserves access to camera ports and controls while cleanly integrating with Peak Design Capture, Peak Design camera straps, and a wide range of third-party accessories.

“The best camera accessories disappear into your workflow until you need them. That idea shaped every decision we made with Field Bracket,” commented Peak Design Founder and CEO, Peter Dering. “Instead of asking photographers to permanently attach functionality they only use some of the time, we built a system that can transform in seconds while remaining just as rigid and dependable as a traditional L-bracket.”

item.title: Exploring perception – and emotion – with Aman Alam
item.description:
From Ozymandias © Aman Alam

Caring for his grandmother, Naseem, as she lived with Alzheimer’s, Aman Alam initially took photographs to comfort himself. But as her condition progressed, the images became a more profound exploration of perception, illness, and love

“This is a pigeon with a baby chick, shot through frosted glass in our bathroom,” says Aman Alam. “I came too close and they felt threatened; probably they’re seeing me as a big shadow just coming towards them. But for me, this image talks about a particular symptom of Alzheimer’s – prosopagnosia [face-blindness], because my grandmother started forgetting faces. 

“When I was there with her, she would know who I was, because she also had my voice, my smell, other senses to complement what she saw of the face. But if she saw a photograph of me, she couldn’t really tell. Then she got progressively worse and worse. Eventually I stopped doing video calls with her, because she would think there were three people on the call – in the bottom right would be her own face, and she wouldn’t recognise herself either. We also removed all the mirrors in the house, because she would get unsettled when she saw her reflection.” 

We’re speaking at Les Rencontres d’Arles, where Alam has an exhibition, Ozymandias, on show until 04 October. But he didn’t start it with an end result in mind. Alam was at university when his grandmother, Naseem, first started to show signs of dementia; years later, when he was 29, her illness progressed and he went back to Agra, northern India, to help care for her. Naseem had been an important early inspiration to Alam, a single mother who was also a history professor and a college principal, and who had fought and negotiated societal norms to carve out an independent life in Agra in the 1970s. Watching her cognitive decline was hard and, searching for more familiar ground and a way to feel like himself, Alam started compulsively carrying his camera.

“What happens in cognitive decline is that parts of your memory are lost, and the brain, to compensate, fills that up with new memories. But the person doesn’t know it’s doing this. To the person that’s their reality.” Aman Alam 

Shooting off images almost as a reflex reaction, he was initially just comforted by the sound of the shutter and pop of the flash; on long walks in the evening, which he took to help clear his mind, he also used the flash to ward off urban animals. Eventually he got interested in the photographs he was unintentionally making, and found to his surprise that they were interesting. Many depict the animals, looming into view from the gloom; others show domestic scenes, verging on the uncanny, unexpectedly lit. The shots evoke something instinctual, or perhaps another way of seeing; disrupting more conventional visual language they suggest alternative views of the world. As Naseem became more confused, more prone to hallucination, confabulation, and fragmentation, questions of perception became ever-more interesting to Alam.

Starting to work on his project more serious, he combined his own images with his family’s archive, particularly studio shots Naseem had enjoyed taking with her daughter (Alam’s mother). Working with Naseem he has coloured some of the old black-and-white images, her insights into the past sharper than her understanding of the present day. Alam also included documentary images of his grandmother’s day-to-day and trips to hospital; there are medical images and brain scans too, showing both alternative imaging techniques and also the progress of her disease. Alzheimer’s can be clearly physically seen, the shifts in perception linked to protein build-ups that stop neurons from communicating with each other. 

Alam also includes a still life image of a walnut, partly because it looks like a brain, partly because his grandmother used to ask for walnuts in place of medicine; I point out Michel Foucault references walnuts in The Order of Things, because in the Renaissance period people believed that nature was shot-through with hidden signs and likenesses, that a walnut could help the brain because it looked like a brain. Alam hasn’t heard the reference before but we’re struck by the connection, the fact that traditional knowledge in Europe and India shares affinities, but also that humans rely on systems of understanding [or ‘epistemes’] to map out the world. 

Alam is aware of how fragile such maps can be, having cared for his grandmother through her cognitive decline; he’s titled his work Ozymandias after the sonnet by Shelley, which describes the impermanence of all things. He’s also included fabulation in his work, leaning into his grandmother’s confabulations rather than trying to steer her out of them. “What happens in cognitive decline is that parts of your memory are lost, and the brain, to compensate, fills that up with new memories,” he explains. “But the person doesn’t know it’s doing this. To the person that’s their reality.

“Whenever my grandmother would confabulate we would correct her, and then she would withdraw into herself, get distant. But I wanted her to talk with me, so I thought ‘Let me just engage, hear her story and validate it’. That made her really happy, and after a few weeks of doing it something miraculous happened – she picked up a newspaper and started reading the headlines. All I had done differently was talking with her and validating her stories, so I contacted the university [treating Naseem] and they said it has not been proven, but they have seen it happen before.”

This insight shaped a conceptual-art installation, The Truth Engine, also on show at Arles. Alam fed family archives, weather reports, environmental data – anything that might help shape a memory – into an LLM, which then confabulated stories, as well as an estimated emotional state. Allowing the AI to create fiction, Alam resisted comparing its narratives with reality. “There’s a thing called hallucination that every AI algorithm tries to do,” he smiles. “In most cases that’s not helpful so we try to curb the hallucination until it sticks to what is right. Instead I said ‘OK you want to confabulate, hallucinate? Go ahead!’” What comes out is 100% fiction, he adds, but it’s all been calculated somehow…

“I wanted to raise questions in a viewer’s mind about what is real, what is fiction, and if the generally accepted version of truth even matters to a mind that believes in its fiction,” he adds. “I wanted to lay stress on how invisible pressures from the present affect a mind connecting fragments from the past. The viewer’s mere presence can become the disturbance that reshapes someone’s past, and by extension their reality.”

Over time the materials Alam amassed multiplied; the hospital presented him with a folder of scans, photographs, and prescriptions, which inspired the dummy book he has made with his work. Titled in three different languages – each in a different script – the dummy includes pages akin to x-rays or the acetates his grandmother used in her lectures; it’s an assemblage of records rather than a straight narrative, suggestive of a folder of evidence. Alam likes the reference but says he’s well aware of other impulses which have shaped what he made, the unconscious pulls and emotional shades which have coloured his work. As with corroborating his grandmothers’ confabulations or the AI’s tall tales, what interests him more is making connections, validating others’ experiences and helping them feel less alone.

Agra was once synonymous with a ‘lunatic’ asylum, set up by the British in the colonial era; its approach is perhaps the direct opposite of Alam’s, and in showing his work, he hopes it will help his viewers and readers. Looking through it together in a hot gallery in a heatwave in France, I feel moved, as many who have lost someone close may also do. I pause to search for the right words and Alam stops and asks, “Would you like to rest for a minute?”

Ozymandias by Aman Alam is on show until 04 October at Les Rencontres d’Arles. Alam won the Serendipity Arles Grant in 2025, which is organised by Serendipity Arts, an international not-for-profit cultural organisation based in India, in collaboration with Les Rencontres d’Arles and supported by Institut Français en Inde.  @alampanah www.rencontres-arles.com/en/expositions/2026/aman-alam

The post White Balance in Photography: The Essential Guide appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Darren Rowse.

And then 2026 came along and changed stuff! We’ve updated this article: How AI has changed white balance in 2026.

White balance. It’s a term that’s thrown around a lot in the world of photography, yet it’s unfortunate how many photographers are left scratching their heads when trying to explain or understand it.

Because here’s the thing: if you want to capture a scene as the human eye perceives it, then white balance should be on your radar. Mastering white balance, both during your shoot and in post-processing, can be the key to more natural-looking photos.

Therefore, in this article, I’m going to share everything you ever wanted to know about white balance, including:

  • The white balance camera settings you should use for consistently good results
  • How white balance can instantly improve your shots
  • How you can use white balance for gorgeous creative effects in your photos

I’m also going to explain key related terms, such as color temperature, white balance presets, and more.

And I promise you: by the time you’ve finished this article, you’ll be an absolute WB expert! Let’s get started.

What is white balance in photography?

White balance refers to the process of removing or neutralizing color casts in your images – because at its core, white balance is about ensuring the colors in your photograph appear as they do in real life.

You see, different light sources emit light with various temperatures and/or tints. Ever noticed how a photo taken under fluorescent lighting sometimes has a blueish hue? Or how shots by candlelight can seem overly warm or yellow? That’s the effect of these different light sources on your images.

Since photographers often want to produce images that look natural, white balancing involves carefully adjusting your camera settings or editing tools to counteract these color casts. It’s about taking an image like this, full of distorted, too-blue colors:

And adding warm colors until you balance out the color cast, so you get a final result like this:

You might be wondering: If lights have such strong color casts, how come I never notice them?

It’s a good question with a simple answer: human eyes are pretty good at correcting for color casts in real time, but a camera captures the subject as it looks in life. Sometimes, the subject will have neutral tones, but other times it’ll be very blue (as in the pear photo above) and sometimes very yellow (as in the pear photo below). In both the blue and the yellow cases, white balancing is necessary to create a neutral image.

Here’s a too-yellow pear photo, which requires significant cooling during the white balancing process:

Note that, during white balancing, you’re adjusting the colors along two spectrums:

  • The blue-yellow spectrum, also known as the color temperature
  • The green-magenta spectrum, also known as the color tint

In general, natural light only requires correction along the blue-yellow spectrum, but certain types of artificial lighting may produce a noticeable color tint, in which case you’ll need to correct for that, too.

Color temperature explained

The bulk of white balancing in photography consists of color temperature correction. You’re correcting for a cast produced by the color temperature of the light, which lies along the blue-yellow spectrum.

Think of it this way: some light sources exude a more yellowish glow, while others lean towards a bluish hue. When we encounter the former, it’s termed a “warm” color temperature. Conversely, the bluish tint signals a “cool” color temperature.

Photographers refer to different color temperatures using the Kelvin scale. Warmer color temperatures, such as those produced by a candle flame or a setting sun, have a low Kelvin value, such as 3000 K. Neutral color temperatures, such as midday sunlight, have a medium Kelvin value – around 5000 K. And cooler color temperatures, produced by clouds or shade, have a high Kelvin value of 6000 K and beyond.

Cooler light has a high Kelvin value? Warmer light has a low Kelvin value?

Yes, you read that right, and it can be confusing, especially if you’ve never encountered the color temperature scale before. But you’ll get used to it over time (and it can help to think of the color temperatures as simply the opposite of what you’d expect).

Why is white balance important?

Color casts cause a couple of problems in photography.

First, they prevent you from capturing accurate, true colors in a scene. If you want to photograph a beautiful red sunset exactly as it appears to your eye, you’ll need to neutralize any color casts; otherwise, your image won’t match the real-life conditions you experienced.

This can also be an issue if you’re doing product photography or real-estate photography, where the goal is to portray the subject as true to life as possible.

Second, color casts tend to look bad. They can mess with portrait skin tones, they can create muddy shadows and sickly highlights, and they can create unwanted moods in your photos.

As I explain later in this article, you can use a color cast for creative effect – but it’s important that you do this carefully and deliberately, rather than as a failure to properly white balance a scene. Make sense?

The two white balancing methods

You can adjust the white balance of your images in two broad ways:

  1. In camera, before taking a shot
  2. Afterward, in post-processing

Both approaches can work, but there are some important caveats to keep in mind:

In-camera white balancing

Most cameras allow you to adjust your white balance settings before ever taking a photo.

For instance, you can select a white balance preset (such as Tungsten, Flash, Cloudy, etc.), which allows your camera to roughly understand and compensate for the lighting conditions.

Some cameras also allow for a custom white balance. Here, you simply dial in a Kelvin value (remember the color temperature scale I shared above?). A high Kelvin value will balance out cooler light and a low Kelvin value will balance out warmer light.

Your camera may even be capable of white balancing off a gray card. Put the gray card in front of your camera, select the right function in the menu, take a picture, and – voila! – your camera will create an accurate color temperature profile of the scene.

But while these white balance options allow you to handle color casts in the field, they come with some drawbacks:

  1. Unless you’re in an enclosed environment, the light will likely change over the course of your shoot. You’ll need to periodically update your white balance preset or redo the gray card process as the sun goes behind clouds, as it sets, etc.
  2. White balance presets, while easy to use, are only approximate. They often won’t produce a perfect result.
  3. If you’re shooting action from a distance, taking a gray card reading is impossible.

That’s why some photographers prefer a different method of white balancing:

White balancing while editing

White balancing in post-processing is pretty simple:

Just set your camera to its Auto White Balance function when out shooting.

Then, when you get back home, open your photos in your editing program of choice.

Most editors offer a similar process, which involves using the white balance eyedropper to identify a neutral tone and fine-tuning via the Temperature and Tint sliders. (Below, I give a step-by-step process for white balancing photos in Lightroom.)

You can white balance each photo individually, or you can create a white balance adjustment for one (or a handful) of photos, then sync the adjustment across the entire set.

After-the-fact white balancing is nice, but like in-camera white balancing, there are a few points you need to keep in mind.

  1. You’ll need to set aside extra time in post-processing to do your white balancing. And while you can save time with batch processing and presets, if you’re capturing lots of images under different lighting conditions, you may prefer the relative ease of in-camera white balancing.
  2. Unless you take photos with a gray card in the frame, you may struggle to get a perfect white balance result with editing. In many cases, that’s fine – the color cast may be barely perceptible – but if you’re photographing products, your client may require literally perfect colors.
  3. For complete white balancing flexibility in editing, you must shoot in RAW. While JPEGs allow for some white balance adjustments, you’ll be limited an often-unacceptable amount – whereas RAW files let you completely set and reset the white balance.

So while post-processing and in-camera white balancing are both serviceable, you’ll ultimately need to choose the option that works best for you.

How AI has changed white balance in 2026

White balance used to be a purely manual judgement call — either picking a preset in-camera or dragging sliders in post. That’s changed a fair bit over the last couple of years.

In-camera scene-aware auto white balance. Most current mirrorless bodies (Canon’s Auto White Balance with “Ambience Priority” vs “White Priority,” Nikon’s Natural Light Auto WB, and Sony’s improved AWB algorithms) now analyze the scene far more intelligently than the “guess the average color” logic of older cameras. They’re genuinely good enough that many photographers now leave AWB on full-time and only override it for tricky mixed-lighting scenes.

Live preview means fewer surprises. If you’re shooting mirrorless, your EVF or rear screen shows you a reasonably accurate preview of your white balance before you press the shutter — a big improvement over the DSLR days of chimping the LCD and guessing.

AI-assisted correction in editing software. Lightroom Classic and Adobe Camera Raw’s “Match Color” and subject-aware tools can now sample skin tones or known-neutral areas across a whole shoot far more reliably than the old single-click eyedropper, particularly useful for batch-correcting a wedding or event shoot with mixed lighting. Capture One and DxO PhotoLab have their own versions of the same idea.

A note for video shooters. If you’re shooting log or flat color profiles for video, white balance works a little differently — you’ll usually want to lock a custom Kelvin value on set rather than relying on auto, since AWB can visibly shift mid-shot. Get it close in-camera and fine-tune in your grade.

None of this replaces understanding the fundamentals below — but it does mean you can lean on your gear more than photographers could even five years ago.

How to white balance using in-camera presets

While white balance presets aren’t the most accurate way to color correct, they’re an easy way to get started (and if you’re simply capturing photos to share on social media, they may be all you require).

Simply pull up your in-camera white balance menu. You should see several presets, such as:

  • Sunny, which works for mid-morning and mid-afternoon sun
  • Shade, which works for scenarios with heavy shade (e.g., portraits under a tree)
  • Cloudy, which works for outdoor scenes featuring overcast lighting
  • Flash, which works for scenes lit by standard off-camera speedlights and pop-up flashes
  • Incandescent, which works for indoor scenes lit by standard warm bulbs
  • Fluorescent, which works for indoor scenes lit by fluorescent bulbs

Then pick the preset that most closely matches the lighting conditions you’re experiencing and start taking photos! You will need to pay close attention to the light as you continue shooting; if it changes significantly, you should switch presets to reflect the new conditions.

How to white balance your photos in Lightroom

Lightroom color correction is a quick and painless process.

First, open an image in the Develop module, then find the WB section on the right-hand side:

Next, select the Eyedropper icon:

Then click on a part of your image that should look a neutral gray or white. (Don’t be afraid to click in a few different places, especially if you’re not sure what counts as “neutral.”)

If you can’t find a neutral area to sample, or you don’t like the results, you can always head over to the Temp and Tint sliders:

You probably won’t need to adjust the Tint slider much, but feel free to drag the Temp slider back and forth until you get a neutral image.

How to creatively use white balance for different effects

While it’s always important to start by color correcting your photos, you can sometimes enhance images by deliberately pushing the white balance in the wrong direction. This generally works best when applied in a post-processing program, not in camera (though you can technically do it either way).

The idea here is simple:

By applying a too-cold white balance to your photos, you can create a somber, moody effect.

And by applying a too-warm white balance to your photos, you can create a welcoming, inviting, even nostalgic effect.

I don’t recommend you push the white balance too far – at some point, your photos may look unnatural – but a bit of cool or warm color is often nice when added carefully.

Note that you can also use an “incorrect” white balance to exaggerate the conditions of the scene. Adding cool hues will give images a shady or night effect, while adding warm hues will give images a sunrise or sunset effect. Again, use this technique with care. It’s easy to go overboard and end up with garish, unpleasant results.

White balance in photography: final words

Now that you’ve finished this article, you’re ready to start adjusting the white balance in your photos so you can capture truly lifelike, authentic images.

Remember, however: don’t be confined by the idea of “correctness.” As with many elements in photography, white balance can also be a tool for artistic expression. Explore, experiment, and embrace the power of white balance to transform the mood and atmosphere of your shots.

So go out with your camera. Practice working with white balance. And make your images shine!

Now over to you:

What do you think about white balance in photography? Do you have any tips for improving your results? Share your thoughts in the comments below!

White balance FAQ

Why is white balance important in photography?

White balance ensures that the colors in your images are accurate and natural. Incorrect white balance can lead to color casts, detracting from the image’s overall quality and authenticity.

What is the difference between white balance and color temperature?

White balance compensates for the color casts produced by either color temperature or color tint shifts. On the other hand, color temperature specifically refers to where the light falls on the blue-yellow spectrum.

How do I know if my white balance is correct?

The simplest indication is when the colors in your image appear natural and true to the scene!

Can you adjust the white balance in post-processing?

Yes, you can. Many editing software options allow for white balance adjustments, giving photographers the flexibility to refine the white balance even after a shot has been taken.
